claim: AMBRA1 is a substrate receptor of a CUL4-RING ubiquitin ligase (CRL4) complex that targets all three D-type cyclins for proteasome-mediated degradation.
source: AMBRA1 is an SR of a CUL4-RING ubiquitin ligase (CRL4) complex that targets all three D-type cyclins for proteasome-mediated degradation (Simoneschi et al., 2021; Chaikovsky et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Simoneschi et al., 2021; Chaikovsky et al., 2021).

claim: The CCND1 gene shows some of the highest frequency of amplification and overexpression among cancer genes across a broad spectrum of human tumors.
source: The CCND1 gene --encoding cyclin D1-- shows some of the highest frequency of amplification and overexpression among cancer genes across a broad spectrum of human tumors (Beroukhim et al., 2010; Curtin et al., 2005; Bignell et al., 2010; Parsons et al., 2008; Jones et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Mutations in CCND1 that prevent the degradation of cyclin D1 by AMBRA1 have been reported in a variety of tumor types.
source: Moreover, mutations in CCND1, which prevent the degradation of cyclin D1 by AMBRA1, a substrate receptor (SR) of a CUL4-RING ubiquitin ligase (CRL4) complex that targets all three D-type cyclins for proteasome-mediated degradation, have been reported in a variety of tumor types (Simoneschi et al., 2021; Chaikovsky et al., 2021; Martínez-Jiménez et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: GTSE1 is a cell cycle-related protein expressed specifically during the S and G2 phases of the cell cycle.
source: GTSE1 is a cell cycle-related protein expressed specifically during the S and G2 phases of the cell cycle (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Liu et al., 2010).

claim: GTSE1 interacts with the tumor suppressor p53 and induces its MDM2-mediated degradation in G2 and during the recovery from DNA damage.
source: It interacts with the tumor suppressor p53, and it induces its MDM2-mediated degradation in G2 and during the recovery from DNA damage, promoting cell proliferation (Liu et al., 2010; Bublik et al., 2010; Monte et al., 2003; Monte et al., 2004; Collavin et al., 2000; Utrera et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: GTSE1 associates with growing microtubules, promoting cell migration.
source: Moreover, GTSE1 associates with growing microtubules, promoting cell migration (Bendre et al., 2016; Scolz et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In prometaphase, GTSE1 becomes highly phosphorylated by CDK1–cyclin B1, resulting in its recruitment to the inner spindle.
source: In prometaphase, GTSE1 becomes highly phosphorylated by CDK1–cyclin B1, resulting in its recruitment to the inner spindle (Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Singh et al., 2021).

claim: After anaphase, GTSE1 dephosphorylation is followed by marked reduction in its abundance in G1.
source: After anaphase, its dephosphorylation is followed by marked reduction in its abundance in G1 (Collavin et al., 2000; Monte et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: GTSE1 emerged as the top hit in orthogonal analyses aimed at identifying proteins whose upregulation in AMBRA1 KO cells was counteracted by Palbociclib treatment.
source: GTSE1, a cell cycle-regulated protein expressed mainly during the G2 and S phases of the cell cycle (Liu et al., 2010), emerged as the top hit in these orthogonal analyses.
evidence: The claim is supported by the bioinformatic analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: High expression of GTSE1 was found to promote the proliferation and invasion of breast cancer cells.
source: Specifically, high expression of GTSE1 was found to promote the proliferation and invasion of breast cancer cells (Lin et al., 2019), and was associated with poor clinical prognosis in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (Lei et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: High expression of GTSE1 was associated with poor clinical prognosis in clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
source: Specifically, high expression of GTSE1 was found to promote the proliferation and invasion of breast cancer cells (Lin et al., 2019), and was associated with poor clinical prognosis in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (Lei et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Lei et al., 2023).

claim: Within multiple cancer cohorts, elevated expression levels of GTSE1 were correlated with a statistically significant poorer prognosis compared to lower expression levels.
source: We explored further the potential influence of GTSE1 on cancer prognosis and found that within multiple cancer cohorts, its elevated expression levels were correlated with a statistically significant poorer prognosis compared to lower expression levels (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Except for acute myeloid leukemia (LAML), GTSE1 expression was higher than that in normal tissue counterparts in all tumor types analyzed.
source: This is noteworthy, since, except for acute myeloid leukemia (LAML), GTSE1 expression was higher than that in normal tissue counterparts in all tumor types analyzed (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic analysis data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: High levels of GTSE1 were found to be prognostically unfavorable across multiple cancer types, presenting a survival pattern similar to that of the cyclin D1–CDK4/6 gene cluster.
source: Similar to the overexpression of other cell cycle-regulated genes (Whitfield et al., 2006), high levels of GTSE1 were found to be prognostically unfavorable across multiple cancer types, presenting a survival pattern similar to that of the cyclin D1–CDK4/6 gene cluster.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with published data on cell cycle-regulated genes and the survival analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: GTSE1 showed an upper shift in a phos-tag gel when co-expressed with cyclin D1–CDK4.
source: GTSE1 showed an upper shift in a phos-tag gel when co-expressed with cyclin D1–CDK4, similar to the known substrates p107 and p130 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GTSE1 underwent phosphorylation by cyclin D1–CDK4, but not by ERK1, in an in vitro phosphorylation assay.
source: The results confirmed that GTSE1 underwent phosphorylation by cyclin D1–CDK4, but not by ERK1, another Pro-directed kinase (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The phosphorylation of GTSE1 by cyclin D1–CDK4 was abolished in the presence of Palbociclib.
source: Moreover, the phosphorylation was abolished in the presence of Palbociclib, similar to the pattern observed with RB (Figure 2B, C, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, C, and H.

claim: Overexpression of Flag-tagged cyclin D1 and CDK4 in HEK293T followed by a Flag pull-down demonstrated binding to endogenous GTSE1.
source: Overexpression of Flag-tagged cyclin D1 and CDK4 in HEK293T followed by a Flag pull-down demonstrated binding to endogenous GTSE1, similar to the canonical substrate RB (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cyclin D1–CDK4 is responsible for the phosphorylation of GTSE1 on four residues (S91, S262, S454, and S724).
source: Our data indicate that cyclin D1–CDK4 is responsible for the phosphorylation of GTSE1 on four residues (S91, S262, S454, and S724).
evidence: The claim is supported by mutagenesis experiments and phos-tag gel analyses shown in Figures 2F and 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A triple mutant of GTSE1 (S91A/S262A/S724A) displayed loss of slower-migrating bands relative to wild-type GTSE1, suggesting diminished phosphorylation.
source: This triple mutant displayed loss of slower-migrating bands relative to wild-type GTSE1, suggesting diminished phosphorylation (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by phos-tag gel data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: A quadruple GTSE1 mutant (S91A/S262A/S454A/S724A) showed complete abrogation of any shift in phos-tag gels.
source: From these two mutants, only the S454A mutation demonstrated a complete abrogation of any shift in phos-tag gels (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by phos-tag gel data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Parental T98G cells displayed a fluctuation in GTSE1 abundance, with low levels in G1 that subsequently increased in S and G2 phases.
source: Parental cells displayed a fluctuation in GTSE1 abundance, with low levels in G1 that subsequently increased in S and G2 phases (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), in agreement with the literature (Collavin et al., 2000; Monte et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle synchronization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and citations to published research.

claim: In AMBRA1 KO T98G cells, GTSE1 levels were consistently elevated throughout the cell cycle.
source: In contrast, in AMBRA1 KO cells, GTSE1 levels were consistently elevated throughout the cell cycle, suggesting that elevated cyclin D1 levels are associated with an increased abundance of GTSE1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle synchronization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: While phosphorylation of GTSE1 in the parental T98G cell line peaked during the G2/M transition, AMBRA1 KO cells exhibited sustained phosphorylation of GTSE1 across all cell cycle phases.
source: Additionally, while phosphorylation of GTSE1 in the parental cell line peaked during the G2/M transition (28–32 hr after serum re-addition), AMBRA1 KO cells exhibited sustained phosphorylation of GTSE1 across all cell cycle phases (Figure 2G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by phos-tag gel and immunoblot data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: An enrichment of GTSE1 phospho-peptides was observed within a pan-cancer cohort as opposed to adjacent, corresponding normal tissues.
source: We observed an enrichment of GTSE1 phospho-peptides within a pan-cancer cohort as opposed to adjacent, corresponding normal tissues (Figure 2I), underscoring the potential role of GTSE1 phosphorylation in tumorigenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by CPTAC data analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Three phosphorylation sites of GTSE1 (S262, S454, and S724) identified as dependent on cyclin D1–CDK4 were statistically enriched in cancers.
source: Upon analyzing single phosphorylated sites, we found that nine were statistically enriched in cancers. Of these, three sites (S262, S454, and S724) were identified as dependent on cyclin D1–CDK4 in our study (Figure 2J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by CPTAC data analysis shown in Figure 2J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Wild-type GTSE1 was found to be phosphorylated in HEK293T cells upon overexpression of all cyclin–CDK pairs tested.
source: Wild-type GTSE1 was found to be phosphorylated in HEK293T cells upon overexpression of all cyclin–CDK pairs, with its shifts in phos-tag gels being abolished upon treatment with the corresponding specific CDK inhibitor (Figure 2H, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by phos-tag gel data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: When the quadruple GTSE1 mutant (Tetra SA) was expressed in HEK293T cells, cyclin D1–CDK4 was unable to induce any shift, whereas the other three cyclin–CDK pairs still sustained phosphorylation.
source: However, when the quadruple (S91A/S262A/S454A/S724A) GTSE1 mutant, referred to as 'Tetra SA', was expressed in HEK293T cells, cyclin D1–CDK4 was unable to induce any shift, whereas the other three cyclin–CDK pairs still sustained phosphorylation (Figure 2H, right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by phos-tag gel data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: An elevation in endogenous GTSE1 levels was observed in AMBRA1 KO cells compared to the parental line.
source: We noticed an elevation in endogenous GTSE1 levels in AMBRA1 KO cells compared to the parental line (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) in agreement with the findings of the proteomic screen performed in AMBRA1 KO cells (Chaikovsky et al., 2021; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, and by proteomic data from Chaikovsky et al., 2021.

claim: A similar increase in GTSE1 levels was observed when overexpressing wild-type cyclin D1 and, even more, an AMBRA1-insensitive, stable mutant of cyclin D1 (T286A).
source: A similar increase was observed when overexpressing wild-type cyclin D1 and, even more, an AMBRA1-insensitive, stable mutant of cyclin D1 (T286A) (Simoneschi et al., 2021; Figure 3A, B), suggesting that the elevated GTSE1 levels are due to high D-type cyclins present in AMBRA1 KO cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: An increase in GTSE1 levels was observed upon acute ablation of AMBRA1 in HCT-116 cells harboring an endogenous fusion of AMBRA1 to a minimally constructed Auxin Inducible Degron (mAID).
source: Again, we observed an increase in GTSE1 levels upon acute ablation of AMBRA1 (i.e., in 8 hr) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The upregulation in GTSE1 abundance in AMBRA1 KO cells was rescued upon Palbociclib treatment.
source: In all cases, the upregulation in GTSE1 abundance was rescued upon Palbociclib treatment (Figure 3A, B), suggesting that this event was a consequence of increased levels of D-type cyclins.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: In the context of AMBRA1 depletion, GTSE1 exhibited a prolonged half-life and reduced degradation rate when compared to control cells in cycloheximide chase assays.
source: The assays revealed that in the context of AMBRA1 depletion, GTSE1 exhibited a prolonged half-life and reduced degradation rate when compared to control cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A parallel half-life assessment in parental U2OS cells and two AMBRA1 KO U2OS clones corroborated the finding that GTSE1 is stabilized in the absence of AMBRA1.
source: A parallel half-life assessment in parental U2OS cells and two AMBRA1 KO U2OS clones corroborated the finding that GTSE1 is stabilized in the absence of AMBRA1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The Tetra SD mutant of GTSE1 exhibited a slower degradation kinetics compared to the Tetra SA mutant and wild-type GTSE1 in cycloheximide chase experiments.
source: Subsequent CHX chase experiments showed a slower degradation kinetics of the Tetra SD mutant compared to the Tetra SA mutant and wild-type GTSE1 (Figure 3E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The Tetra SD mutant of GTSE1 exhibited a statistically significant slower fluorescence decrease rate than both Tetra SA and WT in time-lapse microscopy during a cycloheximide chase.
source: The Tetra SD mutant exhibited a statistically significant slower fluorescence decrease rate than both Tetra SA and WT, indicating reduced degradation (Figure 3G, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: The stabilization of GTSE1 in the presence of MG132 and MLN4924, but not Bafilomycin A, indicates that GTSE1 degradation mainly occurs via the ubiquitin–proteasome system, specifically implicating the involvement of a CRL.
source: The stabilization of GTSE1 in the presence of MG132 and MLN4924, but not Bafilomycin A, indicates that GTSE1 degradation mainly occurs via the ubiquitin–proteasome system, specifically implicating the involvement of a CRL.
evidence: The claim is supported by inhibitor treatment data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: GTSE1 does not appear to be a substrate of CRL4AMBRA1, as indicated by the lack of a physical interaction between AMBRA1 and GTSE1.
source: However, GTSE1 does not appear to be a substrate of CRL4AMBRA1, as indicated by the lack of a physical interaction between AMBRA1 and GTSE1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), as well as the fact that the stabilization of GTSE1 in AMBRA1 KO cells is secondary to the CDK4/6 activity (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and inhibitor treatment data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: GTSE1 abundance and phosphorylation exhibited a statistically significant positive correlation with several proteins integral to cell proliferation, including PCNA, KI67, and MCM2, across multiple cancer cohorts.
source: GTSE1 abundance and phosphorylation exhibited a statistically significant positive correlation with several proteins integral to cell proliferation, including PCNA, KI67, and MCM2, across multiple cancer cohorts.
evidence: The claim is supported by CPTAC data analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GTSE1 levels and phosphorylation demonstrated a negative trend with proteins associated with cell migration and epithelial–mesenchymal transition, such as Vimentin, MMP1, and ETS1, but these did not attain statistical significance.
source: Conversely, in contrast to data suggesting a role for GTSE1 in promoting cell migration (Scolz et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2019; Lei et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2017) GTSE1 levels and phosphorylation demonstrated a negative trend with proteins associated with cell migration and epithelial–mesenchymal transition, such as Vimentin, MMP1, and ETS1, but these did not attain statistical significance.
evidence: The claim is supported by CPTAC data analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and contrasted with published literature.

claim: AMBRA1 KO U2OS cells displayed an enhanced proliferation rate compared to parental cells.
source: AMBRA1 KO cells displayed an enhanced proliferation rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), in agreement with the literature (Simoneschi et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and a citation to published research.

claim: U2OS cells stably expressing the Tetra SD mutant of GTSE1 exhibited a higher proliferation rate compared to cells expressing either Tetra SA or WT GTSE1.
source: Cells stably expressing the Tetra SD mutant exhibited a higher proliferation rate compared to cells expressing either Tetra SA or WT GTSE1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cells harboring the Tetra-SD mutant of GTSE1 displayed an elevated proliferative index, evidenced by a greater number of cell generations and smaller fraction of non-divided cells relative to cells expressing WT GTSE1 and Tetra SA.
source: This was evidenced by a greater number of cell generations and smaller fraction of non-divided cells relative to cells expressing WT GTSE1 and, even more so compared to cells expressing Tetra SA (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by CellTrace dye proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: Expression of a phospho-mimicking GTSE1 mutant induces a decrease in the percentage of cells in G1 and an increase in the percentage of cells in S, similarly to what observed in AMBRA1 KO cells.
source: Finally, cell cycle profiles showed that the expression of a phospho-mimicking GTSE1 mutant induces a decrease in the percentage of cells in G1 and an increase in the percentage of cells in S, similarly to what observed in AMBRA1 KO cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and Rona et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and a citation to Rona et al., 2024.

claim: Amplifications of the CCND1 gene occur in up to 15–20% of breast cancers.
source: Amplifications and overexpression of the CCND1 gene are seen in a diverse array of cancers, with amplifications in up to 15–20% of breast cancers and overexpression in over 50% of mantle cell lymphomas (Musgrove et al., 2011; Cancer Genome Atlas Research, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Overexpression of the CCND1 gene occurs in over 50% of mantle cell lymphomas.
source: Amplifications and overexpression of the CCND1 gene are seen in a diverse array of cancers, with amplifications in up to 15–20% of breast cancers and overexpression in over 50% of mantle cell lymphomas (Musgrove et al., 2011; Cancer Genome Atlas Research, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: GTSE1 is phosphorylated by CDK4 and CDK6 particularly in pathological states, such as cancers displaying overexpression of D-type cyclins.
source: Thus, we propose that GTSE1 is phosphorylated by CDK4 and CDK6 particularly in pathological states, such as cancers displaying overexpression of D-type cyclins.
evidence: The claim is a proposal based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: GTSE1 phosphorylation induces its stabilization, leading to increased levels that contribute to enhanced cell proliferation.
source: In turn, GTSE1 phosphorylation induces its stabilization, leading to increased levels that contribute to enhanced cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data on GTSE1 stability and proliferation assays presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The cyclin D1–CDK4/6-mediated phosphorylation of GTSE1 leads to its increased stability in G1 phase.
source: Our findings demonstrate that the cyclin D1–CDK4/6-mediated phosphorylation of GTSE1 leads to its increased stability in G1 phase, an event that significantly impacts cell proliferation and cancer prognosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The phosphorylation of GTSE1 mediated by cyclin D1–CDK4/6 inhibits GTSE1 degradation, leading to high levels of GTSE1 across all cell cycle phases.
source: The phosphorylation of GTSE1 mediated by cyclin D1–CDK4/6 inhibits GTSE1 degradation, leading to high levels of GTSE1 across all cell cycle phases.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The phosphorylation of GTSE1 promotes cellular proliferation and is associated with poor prognosis within a pan-cancer cohort.
source: Functionally, the phosphorylation of GTSE1 promotes cellular proliferation and is associated with poor prognosis within a pan-cancer cohort.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by proliferation assays and survival analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GTSE1 is a previously unrecognized substrate of cyclin D1–CDK4/6 in tumor cells overexpressing cyclin D1 during G1 and subsequent phases.
source: Here, using an integrative approach combining bioinformatic analyses and biochemical experiments, we show that GTSE1 (G-Two and S phases expressed protein 1), a protein positively regulating cell cycle progression, is a previously unrecognized substrate of cyclin D1–CDK4/6 in tumor cells overexpressing cyclin D1 during G1 and subsequent phases.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: D-type cyclins are activators of the cyclin-dependent kinases CDK4 and CDK6 and represent major oncogenic drivers among members of the cyclin superfamily.
source: D-type cyclins (cyclin D1, cyclin D2, and cyclin D3) are activators of the cyclin-dependent kinases CDK4 and CDK6 and represent major oncogenic drivers among members of the cyclin superfamily (Musgrove et al., 2011; Fassl et al., 2022; Álvarez-Fernández and Malumbres, 2020; Behan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: D-type cyclin-mediated phosphorylation of RB results in the inactivation of its tumor suppressive effect by releasing E2F from the RB's inhibitory effect on gene transcription.
source: D-type cyclin-mediated phosphorylation of RB results in the inactivation of its tumor suppressive effect by releasing E2F from the RB's inhibitory effect on gene transcription.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about RB regulation.

claim: The expression of GTSE1 positively correlates with tumor mutational burden and microsatellite instability in most cancer types.
source: Recent pan-cancer analysis revealed that the expression of GTSE1 positively correlates with tumor mutational burden and microsatellite instability in most cancer types (Tan et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Tan et al., 2023).

claim: Cyclin A2–CDK2, cyclin E1–CDK2, and cyclin B1–CDK1 target additional and/or different sites on GTSE1 compared to cyclin D1–CDK4.
source: In contrast, cyclin A2–CDK2, cyclin E1–CDK2, and cyclin B1–CDK1 target additional and/or different sites as shown by the fact that they still induced mobility shift of the 'Tetra SA' mutant in cultured cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by phos-tag gel data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: In human cells, when D-type cyclins are stabilized in the absence of AMBRA1, GTSE1 becomes phosphorylated across the various cell cycle phases.
source: GTSE1 has been established as a substrate of mitotic cyclins (Liu et al., 2010; Singh et al., 2021; Monte et al., 2000), but we observed that in human cells, when D-type cyclins are stabilized in the absence of AMBRA1, GTSE1 becomes phosphorylated across the various cell cycle phases.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle synchronization data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Overexpression of cyclin D1–CDK4 induces GTSE1 phosphorylation.
source: Accordingly, overexpression of cyclin D1–CDK4 induce GTSE1 phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by phos-tag gel data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The prolonged half-life of GTSE1 consequent to cyclin D1–CDK4-mediated phosphorylation suggests a mechanism through which cells could modulate the abundance of a key regulatory protein without necessitating new protein synthesis.
source: The prolonged half-life of GTSE1 consequent to cyclin D1–CDK4-mediated phosphorylation suggests a mechanism through which cells could modulate the abundance of a key regulatory protein without necessitating new protein synthesis.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data on GTSE1 stability.

claim: A correlation was established between phosphorylation of GTSE1 and markers of cell proliferation, as well as poor prognosis in human cancers.
source: Our study further established a correlation between phosphorylation of GTSE1 and markers of cell proliferation, as well as poor prognosis in human cancers, providing a partial explanatory basis for the proliferative phenotype associated with elevated D-type cyclins observed in human tumors.
evidence: The claim is supported by CPTAC data analysis and survival analysis presented in the manuscript.
